                Constitution Pipeline and Wright Interconnect Projects. Docket Nos. CP13-
                449-006 and CP13-502-003


Dear Secretary Reese,

       Pace Environmental Litigation Clinic, on behalf of our client Stop the Pipeline (STP),
respectfully submits the following comment in response to the Environmental Assessment (EA)
issued by the Federal Regulatory Commission (FERC or the Commission) on August 21, 2026.1
This EA was conducted to assess the environmental effects of the Constitution Pipeline project
(CPP) and Wright Interconnect Project (WIP) (hereinafter, collectively the Project).

        Since its formation in June 2012, STP has been dedicated towards preserving and
enhancing the rural heritage and pristine environment of central New York State and north-
central Pennsylvania by ensuring the purity of its air, water, and soil, the health of its inhabitants,
the resilience of its ecosystems, and the capacity of the area to be self-sustaining. As an
unincorporated association, STP is associated with a thousand people, the majority of whom
would be affected by the proposed pipeline. Some of these members own land along the
proposed pipeline route, while others live, work, or recreate in the area. STP’s interest in this
Project has resulted in the organization’s consistent involvement in the Project since its initiation
in 2012.

    I. BACKGROUND
1
 Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC), Environmental Assessment for the Constitution Pipeline Project
and Wright Interconnect Project, Docket Nos. CP13-499-006 & CP13-502-003, Accession No. 20260821-3005
(Aug. 21, 2026) [hereinafter Environmental Assessment].
         According to the Commission, “the Projects would involve construction and operation of
various project facilities [located] in Susquehanna County, Pennsylvania, and Broome,
Chenango, Delaware, and Schohari Counties” in New York.2 The scope of the Project would be
extensive, with approximately 125 miles of a new 30-inch-diameter natural gas pipeline and
appurtenant facilities, including two new meter stations, ten communication towers, eleven
mainline valves, one pig launcher and receiver, and the expansion of the pre-existing Wright
Compressor Station with an additional 22,000 horsepower of incremental compression and other
modifications. The Project’s footprint would include 1,970.5 acres for construction and 855.3
acres for operation.3 If the Project receives all the necessary approvals, construction of the
Project would begin in the fourth quarter of 2026, with a proposed May 2028 in-service date.4

        On April 3, 2026, the Commission issued a Notice of Scoping Period Requesting
Comments on Environmental Issues for the Proposed Constitution Pipeline and Wright
Interconnect Projects (Notice of Scoping or Notice).5 This Notice resulted in an influx of
comments, including one from STP,6 raising several different issues, including “requests for
restarting the environmental review process, requests to prepare an environmental impact
statement, and objections to Constitution’s petition to affirm New York’s waiver of the water
quality certification requirement under the Clean Water Act.”7 STP’s comment also raised
concerns about the insufficient Final Environmental Impact Statement (FEIS) issued on October
2, 2014.8 Other comments raised concerns over wetland and waterbody crossings, forest clearing
and habitat fragmentation. In its Notice of Schedule, FERC indicated that “all substantive
comments [would] be addressed in its EA.”9

       Instead, FERC merely compiled a list of new or different environmental consequences of
the Project to justify the use of the 2014 FEIS for a 2026 Project.10 This list compared the
environmental effects found in the 2014 FEIS and considers whether any of these effects have
seen any substantial changes.11 FERC found the majority of consequences had no substantial
changes, except for Water Resources, Wetlands, Special Status Species (including State-listed
Species), Land Use, Cultural Resources, Air Quality and Noise, and Reliability and Safety.12
Though the EA claims to address comments the Commission received during the scoping

     II. THE ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT ADDS TO THE INADEQUACIES OF
         THE 2014 FINAL ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT STATEMENT INSTEAD OF
         CURING THEM

        A. FERC Cannot Rely on an Invalid Procedure and a Stale Baseline in its
           Environmental Review

        Because the Second Circuit vacated the underlying Certificate and Waiver Orders and
remanded the proceeding with instructions to dismiss the agency’s proceedings, the Commission
lacks statutory authority to: (1) entertain petitions seeking “reissuance” or “reaffirmance” of
those vacated orders; and (2) rely on the very documents that have been dismissed to conduct its
reviews.13 When an agency order is vacated, it is rendered a legal nullity; it does not remain in
administrative stasis waiting to be revived through summary proceedings.14 The Commission’s
assertion in Table A.4-1 of the 2026 EA15, that the validity of prior orders and legal
reinstatement are issues reserved for the final order, ignores the threshold statutory prerequisite
of NEPA: an environmental review cannot evaluate the “reissuance” of non-existent
authorizations. Treating this proceeding as an expedited continuation of vacated orders and
dismissed dockets, rather than requiring a new Section 7 application with updated resource
reports, unlawfully bifurcates agency review and shields core issues from public scrutiny and the
judicial review that was underway when the Second Circuit vacated the prior orders.

        Even if the Commission had authority to consider the petitions, tying an EA to the 2014
FEIS violates NEPA because the 2014 environmental baseline was structurally deficient when
issued and is now twelve years out of date. In its April 2014 comments on the Draft EIS (DEIS),
STP submitted a detailed accounting (Exhibit 1) demonstrating FERC’s acknowledgement that
essential field surveys, geotechnical borings, and mitigation plans were never completed across
dozens of resource areas.16 Rather than curing these deficiencies in the 2014 FEIS, the
Commission attached over forty post-authorization environmental conditions requiring
Constitution Pipeline, Co., LLC (Constitution), to perform fundamental baseline studies after
certificate issuance.17 A decade later, the 2026 EA perpetuates this flawed structure: staff screens
out core resources in Table A.3-1 by relying on stale, unverified 2014 conclusions, while
attaching 50 conditional requirements that once again defer essential environmental verifications
until after Certificate reissuance.18

         B. FERC Must Incorporate Answers to all Environmental Information Requests in
           its Environmental Review

       Throughout the history of this project, Constitution has engaged in a consistent practice
of evading agency inquiries and promising to deliver critical baseline data only after regulatory
approvals are granted. In December 2013, STP submitted comments documenting how
Constitution systematically deleted or obscured outstanding data requests from the U.S. Army
Corps of Engineers (USACE) and the New York State Department of Environmental
Conservation (NYSDEC) within its tracking tables.19

and June 25, 2026, Environmental Information Requests (EIR Nos. 1 and 2), Constitution
repeatedly refused to provide contemporary field data, asserting that field delineations, species
surveys, and agency coordination would occur only “following reinstatement of the Certificate

        Under NEPA, environmental reviews must be based on comprehensive, upfront baselines
so the public and decision-makers can understand the true environmental consequences before an
irrevocable commitment of resources is made.40 Conditionally granting a certificate while
leaving dozens of essential surveys, delineations, and mitigation plans to be resolved behind
closed doors via post-certificate variance processes violates NEPA’s public participation
requirements.

         C. FERC’s Dismissal of Cumulative Impacts is Arbitrary and Capricious

       The 2026 EA treats cumulative impacts as a minor, isolated checklist, dismissing the
need for an integrated analysis. In doing so, the Commission repeats the errors STP challenged in
2014 and 2015.

         In its April 2014 DEIS comments and its December 2, 2015, request for a Supplemental
Draft EIS (SDEIS), STP demanded FERC evaluate the cumulative and synergistic effects of
regional pipeline development—specifically highlighting Tennessee Gas Pipeline’s (TGP)
Northeast Energy Direct (NED) Project (Docket No. CP16-21), which proposed a parallel supply
path to the same market region.41 In its 2014 Certificate Order, the Commission brushed aside
STP’s cumulative review requests by pointing to divergent in-service dates (claiming
Constitution would enter service in 2015, whereas NED was slated for 2018).42 STP
demonstrated in its December 2015 filing that relying on arbitrary in-service dates when both
projects were simultaneously pending in Commission dockets constituted unlawful segmentation
under Delaware Riverkeeper Network v. FERC.43

        The 2026 EA carries forward this flawed cumulative framework. Section B.1.0 identifies
numerous reasonably foreseeable projects within the regional sub-watersheds—including five
natural gas well development operations, five gas gathering systems, twenty transportation
projects, four industrial developments, and fourteen renewable energy installations.44 Yet, the
EA summarily dismisses these combined effects as “temporary and localized,” concluding
without dynamic hydrologic, ecological, or airshed modeling that cumulative impacts would be
minor.45

        Furthermore, the EA ignores new industrial load sources that did not exist in 2014. In its
May 4, 2026 scoping comments, STP presented evidence that Williams (Constitution’s owner)
has actively acquired equity stakes in power generation facilities to power off-grid, gas-fired AI
data centers.46 With the proposed pipeline route featuring four tap locations capable of feeding
massive regional power generation, the induced development of gas-fired data center

         D. FERC’s Environmental Assessment is Incomplete Without the Required
            Information on Water Resources and Wetlands, and Compliance with Sections
            401 and 404 of the Clean Water Act (“CWA”)

       The 2026 EA fails to provide the site-specific hydrologic analysis required to evaluate
impacts across 330 waterbody crossings and over 91 acres of wetlands.

       In its April 2014 comments, supported by the expert report from Dr. Erik Kiviat and Dr.
David Richardson of Hudsonia Ltd., STP warned that open-cut and dry trenching through 277
streams would trigger severe downstream sedimentation, destroy hyporheic zone nutrient
processing, elevate stream temperatures through riparian clearing, and destabilize steep
headwater catchments.48 Hudsonia emphasized that high-intensity storm events in the Catskill
Plateau exacerbate these disturbances, mobilizing sediments that overwhelm standard silt fencing
and smother trout redds and benthic macroinvertebrate communities.49

        The 2026 EA demonstrates that water resource impacts have expanded rather than
diminished. The number of crossed waterbodies has increased from 289 to 330.50 Key receiving
waters have been afforded higher state protections: Pennsylvania upgraded Roaring Run to Wild
Trout Waters (Natural Reproduction) and Starrucca Creek to Special Protection, while New
York upgraded numerous Class D streams to Class C and B.51 Yet, Constitution has not modified
its crossing methods. It continues to rely on dry open-cut, flume, or dam-and-pump trenching for
235 crossings, relegating horizontal directional drilling (HDD) or Direct Pipe to a fraction of
crossings.52

        The Commission cannot validate this approach by pointing to future Unites States Army
Corps of Engineers (“USACE”) and state permitting. In Section B.2.2, the EA acknowledges that
in a January 9, 2026 letter, Constitution notified the USACE that updated wetland and waterbody
field surveys would be submitted at a “later date”.53 Deferring field delineations to post-

    Constitution also lacks a valid Section 401 Water Quality Certification (“WQC”) from New
York State. After New York denied Constitution’s WQC in 2016 due to insufficient stream
crossing data, Constitution re-applied in May 2025, received three successive Notices of
Incomplete Application from NYSDEC, and withdrew its application on November 7, 2025.55
Constitution’s unilateral assertion in Table 1.7-1 that Section 401 is “Waived” is a contested
legal claim that the Commission cannot rely on to bypass water quality standards.56 The absence
of an active Section 401 application or certification bars the issuance of federal authorizations
under CWA Section 401(a)(1).57

          F. FERC Fails to Address Land Use Conflicts, Direct Workspace Encroachments,
             and Denial of Landowner Due Process

       The passage of twelve years has substantially changed the human and built environment
along the 124-mile route. The 2026 EA documents multiple direct spatial conflicts where new
commercial developments, infrastructure, and residential structures occupy the proposed
construction right-of-way:

        Direct Pipeline Conflicts with Structures: Table B.5-6 of the 2026 EA lists 42
          structures located within 50 feet of the workspace.68 Eight structures—including
          garage/sheds at MP 71.8, MP 78.4, and MP 97.9, and an aboveground storage tank at MP
          4.5—are situated directly over the pipeline centerline or within the workspace (distance =
          0 feet).69 In EIR No. 2, Constitution offered no engineered reroutes, stating only that it
          will coordinate with landowners "at the appropriate time".70 While Staff recognized these
          conflicts by proposing Condition 44 (denying use of PAR-1 because it runs through an
          existing valve facility) and Condition 45 (requiring 10-foot buffers or landowner
          concurrence), NEPA requires that these structural conflicts and routing adjustments be
          resolved and disclosed before authorization, not deferred to private post-certificate
          negotiations.

        New Industrial Developments (Amazon Facility and Active Quarry): The EA
          confirms that a newly constructed 200,000-square-foot Amazon distribution and logistics
          facility at MP 120 directly intersects the pipeline alignment.71 The pipeline would
          traverse approximately 2,000 linear feet of the facility's active truck parking lot and
          stormwater retention basin.72 Similarly, an active 3.2-acre bluestone quarry at MP 6.2
          intersects the proposed right-of-way.73 Constitution has presented no engineered
          realignment or safety risk assessment for these major facilities, and the Commission
          cannot remedy this omission through Condition 50 by directing Constitution to report on
          resolution status in its post-certificate Implementation Plan.

          Due Process of New Landowners: Many parcels along the route have changed hands
           since 2014. In EIR No. 2, FERC Staff identified numerous comment filings from newly
           affected landowners who were never notified of the original proceedings, never
           participated in the 2014 scoping, and purchased land after the Second Circuit was told the
           Projects would not be built.74 Attempting to resurrect expired certificates based on
           outdated scoping denies these property owners their constitutional right to meaningful
           notice and due process under the Natural Gas Act and the Fifth Amendment.75

     III. Conclusion
        The 2026 Environmental Assessment unlawfully relies on a twelve-year-old FEIS located
in a dismissed docket that was incomplete when issued and has been rendered obsolete by
changed environmental conditions and new regulatory standards. By continuously substituting
post-certificate compliance conditions for mandatory upfront baseline surveys across water,
biological, and land resources, the Commission denies the public and affected landowners
meaningful review. The Commission must reject the 2025 and 2026 Petitions and require
Constitution to file a new Section 7 application so that a comprehensive Draft Environmental
Impact Statement can be prepared.
